items.prompt: What group of animals alive today are considered to be dinosaurs?

options.label: Crocodiles and alligators
options.feedback: Crocodiles and alligators are archosaurs related to dinosaurs, but they are not dinosaurs. The only dinosaurs alive today are birds.

options.label: Lizards and snakes
options.feedback: Lizards and snakes are reptiles but not part of the dinosaur group. Birds are the sole surviving lineage of dinosaurs.

options.label: Birds
options.feedback: Correct. Birds evolved from theropod dinosaurs and are the only dinosaur group that survived the extinction event, making them living dinosaurs.

options.label: Turtles and tortoises
options.feedback: Turtles and tortoises are reptiles, but they are not dinosaurs. They belong to a different branch of the reptile family tree.

items.ok_line: Birds are the living descendants of dinosaurs.
items.exp_text: Birds are classified as avian dinosaurs because they evolved from theropod dinosaurs. They are the only dinosaur lineage that survived to the present day, so when we see a bird, we are looking at a dinosaur.

items.prompt: During which era did dinosaurs live?

options.label: The Paleozoic Era
options.feedback: The Paleozoic Era came before the Mesozoic and is known for early life forms like fish and amphibians, not dinosaurs. Dinosaurs appeared in the Mesozoic Era.

options.label: The Mesozoic Era
options.feedback: Correct. Dinosaurs lived throughout the Mesozoic Era, which includes the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods, and they became the dominant land animals during this time.

options.label: The Cenozoic Era
options.feedback: The Cenozoic Era followed the Mesozoic and is the era we are in now. Dinosaurs went extinct at the end of the Mesozoic, except for birds, so they did not live in the Cenozoic.

options.label: The Precambrian Era
options.feedback: The Precambrian Era was billions of years before dinosaurs. Dinosaurs appeared much later, in the Mesozoic Era.

items.ko_line: Dinosaurs are not from those eras.
items.exp_text: Dinosaurs first appeared in the Triassic period and lived through the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods, all of which belong to the Mesozoic Era. They became the dominant land vertebrates during this time.

options.label: Terrible lizard
options.feedback: Correct. The name 'dinosaur' was coined in 1842 and means 'terrible lizard,' referring to the large fossil bones that were first recognized as belonging to these ancient reptiles.

options.label: Ancient reptile
options.feedback: This is close, but the actual meaning of 'dinosaur' is 'terrible lizard.' The name specifically highlights their size and fearsome appearance.

options.label: Giant beast
options.feedback: The name does not mean 'giant beast.' It means 'terrible lizard,' which was chosen because the first fossils looked like huge lizard bones.

options.label: Mighty reptile
options.feedback: The name is not 'mighty reptile.' It is 'terrible lizard,' a term that described the impressive fossil remains found in the 19th century.

items.ko_line: The name has a specific meaning.
items.exp_text: When the first dinosaur fossils were recognized in the early 19th century, the name 'dinosaur' was created. It combines Greek words meaning 'terrible lizard,' a fitting description for the large, lizard-like fossils that were found.

items.prompt: Which of these features is characteristic of all dinosaurs?

options.label: They all had feathers
options.feedback: Not all dinosaurs had feathers. The first dinosaurs likely did not, and feathers only appear in certain groups like theropods. The key shared feature is erect legs.

options.label: They all walked on two legs
options.feedback: Dinosaurs were ancestrally bipedal, but many later groups became quadrupedal, such as sauropods and horned dinosaurs. The defining feature is erect legs, not the number of legs used.

options.label: They were all carnivores
options.feedback: Dinosaurs included both herbivores and carnivores. Some ate plants, others ate meat, and some even ate seeds or fish. The shared feature is the erect leg posture.

options.label: They all had erect legs beneath their bodies
options.feedback: Correct. All dinosaurs had hind limbs held erect beneath their bodies, unlike the sprawling legs of many other reptiles. This is a key feature that defines the dinosaur group.

items.exp_text: Dinosaurs are archosaurs whose hind limbs are held erect beneath the body. This posture is a defining characteristic, while features like feathers, walking on two or four legs, and diet vary among different dinosaur groups.

items.prompt: Which group of dinosaurs includes the largest land animals that ever lived?

options.label: Theropods
options.feedback: Theropods were mostly bipedal carnivores, like Tyrannosaurus, and were not the largest. The largest land animals were the long-necked sauropodomorphs.

options.label: Ceratopsians
options.feedback: Ceratopsians were herbivores with neck frills, like Triceratops, but they were not the largest. Sauropodomorphs hold that record.

options.label: Sauropodomorphs
options.feedback: Correct. Sauropodomorphs were large herbivorous quadrupeds with long necks and tails, and some reached lengths of nearly 40 meters, making them the largest land animals ever.

options.label: Ornithopods
options.feedback: Ornithopods were bipedal or quadrupedal herbivores, like duck-billed dinosaurs, but they were not the largest. Sauropodomorphs were the giants.

items.ok_line: They were the largest land animals.
items.ko_line: Other dinosaurs were not as large.
items.exp_text: Sauropodomorphs are a group of dinosaurs that includes the biggest of all land animals. Some, like Diplodocus and its relatives, could reach over 39 meters in length, thanks to their long necks and tails and massive bodies.

items.prompt: How did dinosaurs like Triceratops and Stegosaurus defend themselves?

options.label: They could fly away
options.feedback: Triceratops and Stegosaurus were land animals and could not fly. Flying dinosaurs, like birds and some theropods, were different. These herbivores used armor or horns.

options.label: They had horns or bony armor
options.feedback: Correct. Many non-avian dinosaurs, including horned dinosaurs like Triceratops and armored dinosaurs like Stegosaurus and ankylosaurs, developed structures such as horns, plates, and bony armor for protection.

options.label: They sprayed poison
options.feedback: There is no evidence that any dinosaur sprayed poison. Defense in these dinosaurs came from physical structures like horns and armor, not chemical weapons.

options.label: They buried themselves in sand
options.feedback: No dinosaur is known to have buried itself in sand for defense. Their adaptations were skeletal, such as horns and armor, not behavioral like hiding underground.

items.ko_line: Flight and poison are not supported.
items.exp_text: Throughout the dinosaur groups, many species showed elaborate structures like horns, crests, and bony armor. These appear to have served as defenses or display features, helping herbivorous dinosaurs like Triceratops and Stegosaurus protect themselves from predators.

items.prompt: What kind of animal is Dimetrodon, often mistaken for a dinosaur?

options.label: A synapsid
options.feedback: Correct. Dimetrodon is a synapsid, which is more closely related to mammals than to reptiles. It is not a dinosaur, even though it looks somewhat similar.

options.label: A dinosaur
options.feedback: Dimetrodon is not a dinosaur. It lacks the erect-leg posture and other features that define dinosaurs, and it belongs to a different group called synapsids.

options.label: A pterosaur
options.feedback: Pterosaurs are flying reptiles related to dinosaurs, but Dimetrodon is not one. Dimetrodon lived on land and is a synapsid, not a pterosaur.

options.label: A marine reptile
options.feedback: Marine reptiles like ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs lived in the sea, but Dimetrodon was a land-dwelling synapsid. It is not a marine reptile.

items.ko_line: It belongs to a different group.
items.exp_text: Dimetrodon is often thought to be a dinosaur, but it is actually a synapsid. Synapsids are the group that includes mammals, and Dimetrodon lived long before dinosaurs. It is not classified as a dinosaur because it lacks the defining features, like erect hind legs.

items.prompt: What did all dinosaurs lay to reproduce?

options.label: Live young
options.feedback: There is no evidence that any dinosaur gave birth to live young. All dinosaurs appear to have laid eggs, based on fossil evidence.

options.label: Hard-shelled eggs only
options.feedback: While many dinosaurs laid hard-shelled eggs, the evidence suggests that all dinosaurs laid eggs, but the shell type varied. The key point is that they all laid eggs, not just some.

options.label: Soft-shelled eggs only
options.feedback: Some dinosaur eggs were soft-shelled, but not all. The consistent trait is that they laid eggs; the shell type differed among species.

options.label: Eggs
options.feedback: Correct. Fossil evidence shows that all dinosaurs, both avian and non-avian, were egg-laying. They did not give birth to live young.

items.exp_text: Evidence indicates that every dinosaur, from the largest sauropod to the smallest bird-like dinosaur, laid eggs. This includes modern birds, which are living dinosaurs and also lay eggs. No dinosaur is known to have had live births.

items.prompt: Which of these animals is NOT classified as a dinosaur?

options.label: Triceratops
options.feedback: Triceratops is a dinosaur, a ceratopsian with a neck frill. It belongs to the ornithischian group of dinosaurs.

options.label: Pterosaur
options.feedback: Correct. Pterosaurs are flying reptiles that are distantly related to dinosaurs, but they are not dinosaurs. They have their own group, Ornithodira, and lack the erect-leg posture of true dinosaurs.

options.label: Stegosaurus
options.feedback: Stegosaurus is a dinosaur, known for the plates on its back. It belongs to the ornithischian group.

options.label: Tyrannosaurus
options.feedback: Tyrannosaurus is a dinosaur, a theropod and a carnivore. It is one of the most well-known dinosaurs.

items.exp_text: Pterosaurs are often mistaken for dinosaurs, but they belong to a separate group of flying reptiles. True dinosaurs are defined by features like erect hind legs, which pterosaurs do not have. Other animals like Triceratops, Stegosaurus, and Tyrannosaurus are all dinosaurs.

items.prompt: What was the typical body size of many non-avian dinosaurs?

options.label: All were enormous
options.feedback: Not all dinosaurs were enormous. While some like sauropods were huge, many were human-sized or even smaller. The variety was extreme.

options.label: All were tiny like birds
options.feedback: Birds are generally small, but many non-avian dinosaurs were large. There were also many small ones, but not all were tiny.

options.label: Many were human-sized or smaller
options.feedback: Correct. Although some dinosaurs were the largest land animals ever, a great number of them were around the size of a human or even smaller. Only some groups like sauropods were gigantic.

options.label: Most were bigger than an elephant
options.feedback: Most dinosaurs were not bigger than an elephant. The giant sauropods were the exception, not the rule. Many were much smaller.

items.exp_text: Dinosaurs showed a wide range of sizes. Some were the largest land animals ever, but many were human-sized or even smaller. The variety in body size was one of the reasons they were so successful.
